title: Classical Mechanics I
source_note: Standard NUC-aligned Nigerian university 200L Classical Mechanics I curriculum: vector kinematics, Newton's laws and their applications, work-energy theorem, linear momentum and collisions, systems of particles and center of mass, rotational dynamics and moment of inertia, angular momentum, central forces and Kepler's laws, gravitation, simple harmonic motion, damped and forced oscillations, and non-inertial reference frames.

questions.question: For a particle moving along a curved path, the velocity vector is always directed
questions.correct_answer: tangent to the path
questions.explanation: Velocity is defined as dr/dt, which points along the direction of instantaneous motion, i.e., tangent to the trajectory.

questions.question: In uniform circular motion, the centripetal acceleration has magnitude a = v^2/r and is directed
options: toward the center of the circle
away from the center of the circle
perpendicular to the plane of motion
questions.correct_answer: toward the center of the circle
questions.explanation: Centripetal acceleration arises from the continuous change in direction of the velocity vector and always points toward the center of the circular path.

questions.question: A projectile is launched with initial speed u at angle theta above the horizontal (no air resistance). Its time of flight is given by
questions.correct_answer: T = 2u sin(theta)/g
questions.explanation: The vertical velocity component u sin(theta) is reduced to zero and reversed by gravity; the total time of flight is twice the time to reach maximum height, giving T = 2u sin(theta)/g.

questions.question: Newton's second law, in its most general form applicable even to variable-mass systems, states that the net force equals
options: the time rate of change of momentum, dp/dt
the product of mass and velocity
the rate of change of kinetic energy
questions.correct_answer: the time rate of change of momentum, dp/dt
questions.explanation: F = ma is only the special case of F = dp/dt when mass is constant; the momentum form is the general statement of Newton's second law.

questions.question: According to Newton's third law, the action and reaction force pair act on
options: neither body, only on the field
questions.correct_answer: two different bodies
questions.explanation: Newton's third law states that for every action force exerted by body A on body B, there is an equal and opposite reaction force exerted by B on A; the two forces act on different bodies and so never cancel for a single object.

questions.question: A block slides down a frictionless incline of angle theta. Its acceleration along the incline is
questions.correct_answer: g sin(theta)
questions.explanation: Resolving gravity along the incline gives a component mg sin(theta), so by Newton's second law the acceleration along the slope is g sin(theta).

questions.question: The work-energy theorem states that the net work done by all forces acting on a particle equals
options: the change in its kinetic energy
the change in its potential energy
questions.correct_answer: the change in its kinetic energy
questions.explanation: Integrating Newton's second law over displacement gives W_net = Delta(KE), the work-energy theorem.

questions.question: A force is conservative if and only if
options: the work it does on a particle moving between two points is independent of the path taken
its magnitude is constant everywhere in space
it acts only on charged particles
it can never do negative work
questions.correct_answer: the work it does on a particle moving between two points is independent of the path taken
questions.explanation: Path-independence of work is equivalent to the force being derivable from a scalar potential (F = -grad U) and having zero curl.

questions.question: A constant net force of 10 N acts on a 2 kg object initially at rest, displacing it 5 m in the direction of the force. What is the object's final kinetic energy?
questions.explanation: Work done W = F*d = 10 N x 5 m = 50 J, and by the work-energy theorem this equals the kinetic energy gained since the object started from rest.

questions.question: In an elastic collision between two particles,
options: both momentum and kinetic energy are conserved
neither momentum nor kinetic energy is conserved
questions.correct_answer: both momentum and kinetic energy are conserved
questions.explanation: An elastic collision is defined precisely as one in which total kinetic energy is conserved in addition to the always-conserved total momentum.

questions.question: In a perfectly inelastic collision, the colliding bodies
options: stick together and move with a common velocity after collision, conserving momentum but not kinetic energy
separate with equal and opposite velocities
conserve both momentum and kinetic energy
have zero total momentum after collision
questions.correct_answer: stick together and move with a common velocity after collision, conserving momentum but not kinetic energy
questions.explanation: In a perfectly inelastic collision the bodies coalesce; momentum is still conserved but some kinetic energy is converted to heat, sound, or deformation.

questions.question: A 1 kg ball moving at 4 m/s collides head-on and sticks to an identical stationary 1 kg ball. What is their common velocity after collision?
questions.correct_answer: 2 m/s
questions.explanation: By conservation of momentum, m1*v1 = (m1+m2)*v_f, so v_f = (1 x 4)/(1+1) = 2 m/s.

questions.question: The moment of inertia of a uniform solid sphere of mass M and radius R about an axis through its center is
questions.explanation: Integrating the mass distribution of a uniform solid sphere about a diameter gives the standard result I = (2/5)MR^2.

questions.question: The moment of inertia of a thin uniform ring (hoop) of mass M and radius R about an axis through its center, perpendicular to its plane, is
questions.correct_answer: MR^2
questions.explanation: Every mass element of a thin hoop lies at the same distance R from the central axis, so I = integral(r^2 dm) = MR^2.

questions.question: The rotational analogue of Newton's second law, relating net torque tau to angular acceleration alpha, is
questions.correct_answer: tau = I*alpha
questions.explanation: Just as F = ma governs linear motion, tau = I*alpha governs rotational motion, with moment of inertia I playing the role of rotational inertia.

questions.question: The parallel axis theorem for moment of inertia states that I = I_cm + Md^2, where d is
options: the perpendicular distance between the new axis and the axis through the center of mass
the distance from the axis to the edge of the body
the total length of the body
questions.correct_answer: the perpendicular distance between the new axis and the axis through the center of mass
questions.explanation: The parallel axis theorem relates the moment of inertia about any axis to the moment about a parallel axis through the center of mass plus Md^2, where d is the perpendicular separation between the two parallel axes.

questions.question: An ice skater spinning with arms outstretched pulls her arms in. Assuming negligible external torque, her angular velocity
options: increases, since angular momentum L = I*omega is conserved and I decreases
stays the same, since L is not conserved
questions.correct_answer: increases, since angular momentum L = I*omega is conserved and I decreases
questions.explanation: With no external torque, angular momentum L = I*omega is conserved; reducing the moment of inertia I by pulling in the arms forces omega to increase.

questions.question: The angular momentum of a particle about a point is defined as
options: L = r x p, the cross product of its position and linear momentum vectors
L = r . p, the dot product of position and momentum
questions.correct_answer: L = r x p, the cross product of its position and linear momentum vectors
questions.explanation: Angular momentum about a chosen origin is defined as the cross product of the position vector and the linear momentum vector.

questions.question: Kepler's second law (equal areas swept in equal times by a planet's radius vector) is a direct consequence of
options: conservation of angular momentum under a central force
questions.correct_answer: conservation of angular momentum under a central force
questions.explanation: Since gravity is a central force producing zero torque about the Sun, angular momentum L = m*r^2*(dtheta/dt) is constant, which is equivalent to the radius vector sweeping out equal areas in equal times.

questions.question: Kepler's third law states that the square of a planet's orbital period is proportional to
options: the cube of the semi-major axis of its orbit
the square of the semi-major axis
questions.correct_answer: the cube of the semi-major axis of its orbit
questions.explanation: Kepler's third law, T^2 proportional to a^3, follows from applying Newton's law of gravitation to a body in a bound orbit around a much larger central mass.

questions.question: A central force acting on a particle is one that
options: is always directed along the line joining the particle to a fixed center and depends only on the distance r
always points in a fixed direction in space
depends on the particle's velocity only
acts perpendicular to the position vector
questions.correct_answer: is always directed along the line joining the particle to a fixed center and depends only on the distance r
questions.explanation: By definition a central force F(r) = f(r)*r-hat is radial and its magnitude depends only on the separation r from the force center, which is why it produces zero torque about that center.

questions.question: For two particles of masses m1 and m2 interacting via a central force, the reduced mass used to convert the problem into an equivalent one-body problem is defined as
questions.explanation: Separating the two-body problem into center-of-mass and relative motion shows the relative coordinate obeys the equation of a single particle of reduced mass mu = m1*m2/(m1+m2) moving under the interaction force.

questions.question: Newton's law of universal gravitation states that the gravitational force between two point masses is
options: directly proportional to the product of the masses and inversely proportional to the square of their separation
directly proportional to the sum of the masses and the separation
inversely proportional to the product of the masses
questions.correct_answer: directly proportional to the product of the masses and inversely proportional to the square of their separation
questions.explanation: Newton's law of gravitation is F = G*m1*m2/r^2, an inverse-square law in the separation r and directly proportional to each mass.

questions.question: The minimum speed needed for an object to escape a planet's gravitational field from its surface, ignoring air resistance, is
questions.correct_answer: v = sqrt(2GM/R)
questions.explanation: Escape velocity is found by setting the total mechanical energy (kinetic plus gravitational potential) equal to zero at infinity, giving v_esc = sqrt(2GM/R).

questions.question: The gravitational potential energy of two point masses M and m separated by distance r, taking U = 0 at infinite separation, is
questions.correct_answer: U = -GMm/r
questions.explanation: Integrating the attractive gravitational force with the convention U(infinity) = 0 gives the negative potential energy U = -GMm/r.

questions.question: A particle undergoes simple harmonic motion if its acceleration satisfies
options: a = -omega^2*x, i.e., acceleration is proportional to and directed opposite to displacement
questions.correct_answer: a = -omega^2*x, i.e., acceleration is proportional to and directed opposite to displacement
questions.explanation: This defining differential equation, a restoring acceleration proportional to displacement from equilibrium, has the general solution x(t) = A cos(omega*t + phi).

questions.question: The period of a simple pendulum of length L undergoing small oscillations is
questions.correct_answer: T = 2*pi*sqrt(L/g)
questions.explanation: For small angular displacements, the pendulum's equation of motion reduces to SHM with angular frequency omega = sqrt(g/L), giving period T = 2*pi*sqrt(L/g).

questions.question: For a mass-spring system undergoing SHM with amplitude A and spring constant k, the total mechanical energy is
options: (1/2)kA^2, and remains constant throughout the motion
(1/2)kA^2, but decreases as the mass moves toward equilibrium
questions.correct_answer: (1/2)kA^2, and remains constant throughout the motion
questions.explanation: In ideal (undamped) SHM, kinetic and potential energy continuously interconvert but their sum, (1/2)kA^2, remains constant since no energy is dissipated.

questions.question: A damped oscillator is said to be critically damped when it
options: returns to equilibrium in the shortest time possible without oscillating
takes an infinitely long time to reach equilibrium while oscillating
questions.correct_answer: returns to equilibrium in the shortest time possible without oscillating
questions.explanation: Critical damping is the boundary case between underdamping (oscillatory decay) and overdamping (slow non-oscillatory decay) and gives the fastest non-oscillatory return to equilibrium.

questions.question: Resonance in a forced, lightly damped oscillator occurs when
options: the driving frequency is close to the system's natural frequency, producing maximum amplitude
the driving frequency is much greater than the natural frequency
questions.correct_answer: the driving frequency is close to the system's natural frequency, producing maximum amplitude
questions.explanation: When the driving frequency approaches the natural (undamped) frequency of the system, the steady-state amplitude of forced oscillation reaches a sharp maximum, a phenomenon called resonance.

questions.question: An overdamped oscillator, compared to a critically damped one,
options: returns to equilibrium more slowly without oscillating
reaches equilibrium in the shortest possible time
questions.correct_answer: returns to equilibrium more slowly without oscillating
questions.explanation: Overdamping corresponds to very large damping; the system still does not oscillate, but it approaches equilibrium more slowly than in the critically damped case.

questions.question: The Coriolis force experienced by an object moving in a rotating reference frame is
options: a fictitious force proportional to the object's velocity relative to the rotating frame, perpendicular to that velocity
a real force acting only on charged particles
proportional to the square of the angular velocity only
questions.correct_answer: a fictitious force proportional to the object's velocity relative to the rotating frame, perpendicular to that velocity
questions.explanation: The Coriolis pseudo-force, -2m(omega x v'), appears only for objects moving relative to a rotating frame and acts perpendicular to both the rotation axis and the relative velocity.

questions.question: The centrifugal force in a rotating reference frame is a fictitious (pseudo) force that
options: appears to push objects outward, away from the axis of rotation, and exists only in the rotating (non-inertial) frame
is a real force that exists in all reference frames
acts toward the axis of rotation in the rotating frame
only affects objects at rest in the inertial frame
questions.correct_answer: appears to push objects outward, away from the axis of rotation, and exists only in the rotating (non-inertial) frame
questions.explanation: Centrifugal force is introduced to make Newton's second law work in a rotating frame; it has no counterpart force pair and vanishes when viewed from an inertial frame.

questions.question: A reference frame is called inertial if
options: Newton's first law holds in it, i.e., it is not accelerating relative to other inertial frames
it is always at rest relative to Earth
fictitious forces must be added to describe motion within it
questions.correct_answer: Newton's first law holds in it, i.e., it is not accelerating relative to other inertial frames
questions.explanation: An inertial frame is one in which a body free of net force moves at constant velocity (Newton's first law); accelerating or rotating frames are non-inertial and require fictitious forces.

questions.question: The center of mass of a system of particles moves as though
options: all the mass were concentrated there and all external forces were applied there
it were fixed in space regardless of external forces
the total momentum of the system depends on internal forces only
each particle's individual motion is duplicated at that point
questions.correct_answer: all the mass were concentrated there and all external forces were applied there
questions.explanation: Summing Newton's second law over all particles shows that internal forces cancel in pairs (Newton's third law), leaving M*a_cm = F_external, so the center of mass behaves like a single particle of the total mass under the net external force.
